notes: Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; clean, low-fermentation washed processing is the best-documented case with the most consistent guidance across roasters.
Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; some mucilage sugar left on the bean during drying adds a modest fermentation load beyond washed.

Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; whole-cherry drying adds sugar/fruit compounds and traps extra CO2, extending both the wait and the usable window versus washed.

Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; hulling at high moisture yields a low-density, low-acid bean that specialty sources describe as best enjoyed very fresh, needing little rest.

Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; a sealed anaerobic soak before washing adds a moderate fermentation load on top of an otherwise clean washed process.

Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; sealed, oxygen-free fermentation produces stronger, sometimes 'funky' aromatics that many roasters say benefit from extra rest to settle.

Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; combining whole-cherry drying with anaerobic fermentation compounds two intense variables, so evidence here is thinner and more producer-dependent.

Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; whole-cherry CO2-flush fermentation (borrowed from winemaking) is anecdotally reported to need extended rest, sometimes 3+ weeks, before flavors settle.

Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; carbonic maceration layered onto a full natural dry-down is among the most fermentation-intense combinations modeled, with the least standardized guidance.

Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; rapid temperature cycling to rupture cell walls is a newer technique with very little published resting guidance, so this is an estimate by analogy to other intense ferments.

Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; Aspergillus oryzae inoculation is a novel technique with almost no published resting-time guidance; treated here like other intense, unsettled ferments.

Light roasts are dense and less porous, so CO2 escapes slowly and flavor keeps developing for days; targeted lactic-acid-bacteria fermentation produces a strong tangy/funky character that anecdotal roaster guidance says needs real time to integrate.
